title: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Learn about the role of the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) in administering and reviewing R&D claims in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is the single federal agency that administers Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program under the Income Tax Act, evaluating both technical eligibility and financial expenditures. Taxpayers claiming SR&ED must file Form T661 and supporting schedules with the CRA within 18 months of their taxation year-end.

body.text: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is the single federal agency that administers Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program under the Income Tax Act, evaluating both technical eligibility and financial expenditures. Taxpayers claiming SR&ED must file Form T661 and supporting schedules with the CRA within 18 months of their taxation year-end.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Incentive Landscape

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive fiscal regimes for supporting industrial research, scientific inquiry, and technological innovation. The cornerstone of this architecture is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which is jointly structured by the Department of Finance Canada and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) pursuant to the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Rather than functioning as a discretionary grant with a fixed budgetary appropriation, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive integrated directly into the corporate and personal income tax systems. Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs work satisfying the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and complies with the prescribed reporting deadlines under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) is legally entitled to claim both an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable income deduction under section 37 and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under sections 127 and 127.1.

Between late 2024 and late 2026, the Canadian R&D tax incentive landscape underwent its most consequential structural expansion in over a decade. Following policy consultations initiated in Budget 2024 and preliminary proposals announced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement—which initially contemplated raising the enhanced expenditure limit to $4.5 million—the federal government enacted sweeping legislative reforms through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from the historical 10,000,000–50,000,000 range to a new 15,000,000–75,000,000 range, introduced an alternative three-year average gross revenue phase-out election, extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs for property acquired after December 15, 2024.

Building upon the enactment of Bill C-15, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026 through My Business Account, providing claimants with upfront technical eligibility determinations within an eight-week service standard prior to tax return filing. Subsequently, on November 5, 2026, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled Federal Budget 2026, which retained the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and capital expenditure restoration while proposing two further structural pillars: first, an expansion of the SR&ED regime, proposed to apply for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (January 1, 2027 for calendar-year corporations), to cover commercialisation-adjacent costs including regulatory approval studies and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses; and second, a permanent Productivity Mega Deduction that would provide immediate full capital write-offs across more than 65% of business investment, reducing Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment from 13.0% to 6.4%. Simultaneously, provincial jurisdictions recalibrated their complementary R&D tax credits, highlighted by Quebec's transition to the unified refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialisation (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and British Columbia's enactment of Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), which made the British Columbia SR&ED tax credit permanent and aligned its refundable expenditure limit and capital rules with the federal $6,000,000 framework.

body.text: Federal Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution
The Dual-Mechanism Structure of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED incentive operates through a two-stage statutory mechanism embedded within Part I of the Income Tax Act. The first stage governs the deduction of SR&ED expenditures in computing net income for tax purposes under section 37, while the second stage governs the generation, application, carryback, carryforward, and cash refundability of Investment Tax Credits under sections 127 and 127.1.

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act—specifically including paragraphs 37(1)(a), (b), (d), and (e), alongside timing rules in subsection 37(1.2)—a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may deduct current SR&ED expenditures and, following the repeal of pre-2024 capital restrictions, qualified capital expenditures on property acquired after December 15, 2024, incurred in Canada that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED. Rather than deducting these expenses under the general business profit computation rules of section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a), qualifying expenditures are aggregated into a dedicated, cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 37(1). Any unclaimed balance in the subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year does not expire; instead, it carries forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in any subsequent taxation year at the taxpayer's discretion. Crucially, any federal or provincial SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in a given taxation year reduces the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e), preventing a double fiscal benefit while preserving the full current-year expenditure deduction.

The second stage is governed by subsections 127(5) through 127(11.2) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 127(5) permits a taxpayer to deduct its accumulated "investment tax credit" (defined in subsection 127(9)) from its Part I tax otherwise payable. To the extent that a non-refundable ITC exceeds the taxpayer's Part I tax liability in the current taxation year, the unused credit may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the earlier year's Part I tax remaining after that year's credits) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Where the claimant qualifies for cash refundability under section 127.1, subsection 127.1(3) deems any SR&ED ITC refunded to the taxpayer in the taxation year to have been deducted under subsection 127(5) against Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby extinguishing that portion of the credit from the carryforward and carryback pool.
Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 ITC is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" housed in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, rather than in section 127, which governs expenditure quantification and credit calculation once technical eligibility is settled, or subsection 127(11.1), which reduces the qualified expenditure pool for government assistance and contract payments. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four enumerated qualifying branches.

The first branch, set out in paragraph (a) of the definition in subsection 248(1), encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second branch, set out in paragraph (b), encompasses applied research, which is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and quantitatively largest branch, set out in paragraph (c), covers experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The fourth branch, set out in paragraph (d), covers eligible support work, which consists of work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes routine, commercial, and non-technological activities from qualifying as SR&ED, even when performed by qualified scientists or software engineers. Specifically, routine software coding, bug fixes, standard engineering design, quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, market research or sales promotion, research in the social sciences or the humanities, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, style changes, and routine data collection fail the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) because they do not seek to resolve genuine scientific or technological uncertainty through systematic experimentation or analysis.
Legislative Trajectory: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 and Budget 2026

A rigorous technical audit of Canadian R&D tax documentation requires distinguishing among three distinct policy milestones that occurred between 2024 and 2026: the initial consultation parameters and the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), the enacted provisions of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), and the prospective expansions tabled in Federal Budget 2026.

In early 2024, the Department of Finance launched public consultations to modernise the SR&ED program, focusing on whether the non-refundable basic rate, the expenditure cap, the CCPC-only restriction for the refundable credit, and the taxable capital phase-out limit remained globally competitive. On December 16, 2024, the Fall Economic Statement—subsequently reflected in the August 2025 Department of Finance draft legislative explanatory notes—initially proposed raising the expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, expanding the taxable capital phase-out range to 15,000,000–75,000,000, extending the enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditures. However, in Budget 2025 and the resulting implementation legislation—Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (enacted as S.C. 2026, c. 3)—Parliament superseded the interim $4,500,000 proposal and doubled the enhanced expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs and ECPCs, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Consequently, any advisory commentary or legacy text referencing a $3,000,000 or $4,500,000 expenditure limit for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 is legally inaccurate under enacted subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (dated October 7, 2026).

The statutory amendments enacted by Bill C-15 restructured multiple interdependent subsections of section 127 and section 127.1 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. In subsection 127(9), Parliament added the statutory definitions of "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) and "eligible subsidiary", alongside transitional application rules in subsections 127(9.01) and 127(9.02). Subsection 127(10.1), which provides the enhanced 20% ITC addition on top of the 15% basic ITC, was amended to apply not only to a corporation that was a CCPC throughout the taxation year, but also to a corporation that was an ECPC throughout the taxation year. Subsection 127(10.2) was amended to replace the legacy $3,000,000 expenditure limit and 10,000,000–50,000,000 taxable capital taper for CCPCs with a $6,000,000 expenditure limit and a 15,000,000–75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital taper. Furthermore, new subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) were enacted to allow a single CCPC (subsection 127(10.31)) or a group of associated CCPCs (subsection 127(10.32)) to elect out of the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute the expenditure limit using the three-year average annual gross revenue formula in subsection 127(10.6).

To accommodate the new ECPC rules within section 127, Bill C-15 renumbered former subsection 127(10.6) as subsection 127(10.5), which continues to govern expenditure limit determinations in special cases such as short taxation year prorations (paragraph 127(10.5)(b)) and multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year. Newly enacted subsection 127(10.6) establishes the expenditure limit formula based on three-year average gross revenue for ECPCs and revenue-electing CCPCs. Parallel to the associated CCPC rules in subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4), Parliament enacted subsections 127(10.61), 127(10.62), 127(10.63), and 127(10.64) to govern expenditure limit sharing among consolidated ECPC groups (cross-referencing the definition of "Consolidated Financial Statements" in subsection 233.8(1)), allocation agreements, Ministerial allocations upon failure to file an agreement, and specific application rules. Simultaneously, Bill C-15 repealed paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1) and amended acquisition timing rules in subsection 127(11.2) and refundability rules in section 127.1 to restore SR&ED capital expenditures (at a 40% cash refundability rate within the expenditure limit) and lease costs in respect of property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease payments that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024.

On November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 proposed the next wave of legislative reforms. For taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day (November 5, 2026, meaning January 1, 2027 for calendar-year corporate filers), the SR&ED program would be expanded to include two previously excluded downstream commercialisation categories: first, tests and studies conducted for the purpose of obtaining regulatory approval or certification; and second, intellectual property protection costs, specifically covering patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. In addition, following draft legislative proposals released on September 15, 2026, Budget 2026 confirmed the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction, which would enable businesses of all sizes to immediately write off 100% of the capital cost of eligible depreciable assets across more than 65% of business investment (up from roughly 15%), subject to exclusions for certain long-lived buildings, passenger vehicles, regulated natural gas distribution pipelines, and resource-depletion property.

body.text: Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Mechanics, and Refundability
The Enhanced 35% Rate versus the Basic 15% Rate

The federal SR&ED ITC operates on a two-tier rate structure defined in subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act. The baseline "specified percentage" defined in subsection 127(9) is the 15% basic ITC rate. This 15% basic rate applies to corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinational corporations, or public corporations that do not meet the ECPC definition), to CCPCs and ECPCs on the slice of their qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, and to unincorporated taxpayers including individuals (sole proprietorships), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts.

Conversely, subsection 127(10.1) provides an additional 20% credit on top of the 15% basic rate, creating a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, this 35% enhanced rate is available to both Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) (as defined in subsection 125(7)) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (as defined in subsection 127(9)). With the maximum expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 under Bill C-15, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC can generate up to $2,100,000 in enhanced federal ITCs per taxation year, compared to a maximum of $1,050,000 under the pre-reform $3,000,000 cap.

To qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) throughout a taxation year under subsection 127(9), a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory criteria. First, the corporation must be resident in Canada and must be a taxable Canadian corporation throughout the taxation year. Second, the corporation must be a public corporation—generally meaning its shares are listed on a designated Canadian or foreign stock exchange such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ—and must not be a CCPC. Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, or it must qualify as an "eligible subsidiary" of an ECPC parent under subsection 127(9), thereby preserving the domestic Canadian control policy standard across publicly traded entities.
Statutory Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital and Gross Revenue Tests

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit is subject to a gradual linear phase-out based on corporate size. Crucially, a widespread misconception in legacy tax commentary is that prior-year federal taxable income reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure limit. In fact, Parliament repealed the federal taxable income phase-out from subsection 127(10.2) in earlier legislative cycles; consequently, prior-year taxable income does not enter the expenditure limit formula in subsection 127(10.2). Instead, the federal expenditure limit is phased out strictly by reference to either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual gross revenue.
1. The Default CCPC Taxable Capital Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC files a revenue election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32), its annual expenditure limit for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 is determined by the statutory formula in subsection 127(10.2): Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000.

Within this statutory formula, variable A is nil ($0) if the total taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning assigned by section 181.2 of Part I.3) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, variable A is equal to the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, expressed mathematically as A = lesser of $60,000,000 and (prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada − $15,000,000). Mathematically, the $60,000,000 denominator applied against a $6,000,000 expenditure limit creates a linear 1:10 reduction ratio: every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above the $15,000,000 threshold cuts the CCPC's expenditure limit by $100,000, until the expenditure limit reaches nil ($0) at $75,000,000 of taxable capital.
2. The ECPC and Electing-CCPC Gross Revenue Formula (Subsection 127(10.6))

Because public corporations and certain capital-intensive private enterprises often carry substantial balance-sheet equity or debt while generating modest revenue, subsection 127(10.6) establishes an alternative revenue-based phase-out formula that is mandatory for ECPCs and elective for CCPCs under subsections 127(10.31) (for a single CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a group of associated CCPCs). While the August 2025 draft explanatory notes reflected the interim $4,500,000 FES figure, enacted Bill C-15 harmonized the enhanced expenditure limit at $6,000,000 across the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 three-year average gross revenue corridor. Under subsection 127(10.6), variable A is computed using the total of all amounts of average annual gross revenue reflected in the financial statements (or Consolidated Financial Statements as defined in subsection 233.8(1) for consolidated ECPC groups under subsection 127(10.62)) of each corporation in the associated or consolidated group over the three preceding fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated or consolidated throughout the entirety of that three-year period.

Where a CCPC is asset-heavy—such as a biotechnology developer, clean-energy pilot facility, or deep-tech hardware startup that has raised $45,000,000 in equity or debt financing (which increases Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada to $45,000,000 and cuts its subsection 127(10.2) limit in half to $3,000,000) but has average annual gross revenue of $15,000,000 or less—filing the election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) disapplies subsection 127(10.2), preserves the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6), and rescues up to $600,000 in additional refundable tax credits ($3,000,000 × 20% rate differential).

body.text: Associated Corporations, Consolidated Groups, and Short Taxation Years

To prevent corporate groups from multiplying the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by incorporating multiple subsidiaries, subsection 127(10.21) deems the expenditure limit of an associated CCPC to be nil ($0) unless all associated corporations in the group file an agreement in prescribed form (Schedule 49, Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3) allocating the group's single shared expenditure limit among its members. If the associated corporations fail to file the allocation agreement, subsection 127(10.4) empowers the Minister of National Revenue to allocate the expenditure limit among the members of the group. Parallel rules apply to consolidated ECPC groups under subsections 127(10.61), 127(10.62), and 127(10.63). Furthermore, paragraph 87(2)(j.6) enforces corporate continuity upon an amalgamation, deeming the new corporation formed as a result of an amalgamation to be the same corporation as, and a continuation of, each predecessor corporation for the purposes of subsection 127(10.2). Conversely, subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23) govern specific applications of deemed non-association of corporations, while subsection 127.1(2.2) coordinates refundable ITC rules across associated CCPCs.

Where a corporation has a short taxation year—defined in paragraph 127(10.5)(b) as a taxation year of less than 51 weeks—or has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in the same calendar year, subsection 127(10.5) mandates a strict proration of the corporation's expenditure limit based on the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365: Prorated Expenditure Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in the Taxation Year ÷ 365).

For example, as illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if Corporation P is allocated $3,000,000 of an associated group's expenditure limit and has a short taxation year running from July 1 to December 31 (184 days), its prorated expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is $3,000,000 × 184 ÷ 365 = $1,512,329.
Refundability Mechanics Under Section 127.1

Earning an ITC under section 127 does not automatically entitle a claimant to a cash refund; cash refundability is governed separately by section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act and turns upon three variables: first, the legal classification of the claimant (Qualifying CCPC, Non-Qualifying CCPC, ECPC, Other Corporation, or Individual/Trust); second, whether the expenditure falls within or above the corporation's annual expenditure limit; and third, whether the expenditure is of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount and eligible equipment lease payments) or of a capital nature (purchased depreciable equipment).

While prior-year taxable income no longer reduces the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2), prior-year taxable income remains determinative of whether a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" under section 127.1—which requires that the CCPC's prior-year taxable income, combined with all associated corporations, does not exceed its "qualifying income limit". Under Bill C-15, the qualifying income limit—$500,000, reduced on a straight-line basis as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises—is phased out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of taxable capital (previously $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Qualifying corporation status determines whether a CCPC receives a 40% cash refund on its 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit; a CCPC whose prior-year group taxable income exceeds its qualifying income limit is not a qualifying corporation for that slice and receives 0% cash refundability above the expenditure limit, meaning 100% of its 15% basic credit must be applied against Part I tax or carried back 3 years / forward 20 years. Similarly, for an ECPC, expenditures above the expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC on a non-refundable basis (0% cash refundability).

body.text: Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
Directly Engaged Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada form the primary expenditure base of most claims. For arm's-length employees, 100% of the portion of salaries and wages directly attributable to time spent on hands-on SR&ED activities—including experimental design, hypothesis testing, prototype construction, and commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d)—is includable in the section 37 expenditure pool. However, the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations impose two distinct layers of anti-avoidance restrictions on "specified employees", defined broadly as employees who own, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation) or who do not deal at arm's length with the employer.

Under the first layer of restriction, governing direct SR&ED salary inclusion in the expenditure pool, a specified employee's includable SR&ED remuneration cannot include any bonus, profit-based remuneration, or taxable benefits, and total includable salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was employed. Under the second and more restrictive layer, governing the computation of the "salary base" upon which the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) narrow the proxy salary base substantially. Specifically, for all employees (arm's-length and specified alike), bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits are excluded from the proxy salary base. Furthermore, for a specified employee, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) cap the amount includable in the proxy salary base at the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary and wages (allocated to SR&ED time) and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days employed in the taxation year. For a taxation year ending in 2026, this proxy salary base ceiling is $186,500.
Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55%) vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election in Part 3 of Form T661 to compute SR&ED overhead and other expenditures using either the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (selected on Line 160) or the Traditional Method (selected on Line 162). Once filed for a given taxation year, the choice is binding and cannot be changed for that taxation year.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, governed by subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the taxpayer does not track or itemise actual SR&ED overhead expenses. Instead, the taxpayer computes a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 and entered at Line 502 in Part 4). Technical auditors must guard against a recurring error found in outdated commentary claiming a 65% proxy rate: the PPA rate was 65% for taxation years up to 2012, 60% in 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since 2014. Using the outdated 65% rate overstates notional overhead by ten percentage points and is automatically adjusted upon CRA assessment. Moreover, because the PPA is a notional calculation, it is excluded from the section 37 income deduction pool; it counts solely toward the qualified expenditure pool in Part 4 of Form T661 for computing the section 127 ITC.

Under the Traditional Method, the taxpayer foregoes the 55% notional proxy and instead identifies, itemises, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning the costs would not have been incurred but for the execution of the SR&ED work. Unlike the PPA, actual overhead expenditures substantiated under the Traditional Method are added to both the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the section 127 ITC qualified expenditure base.
The Cloud Computing and Software Subscription Audit Trap

A critical area of audit friction in modern software, artificial intelligence (AI), and data analytics claims involves the classification of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud compute clusters) and specialised software subscriptions. Although informal industry blogs occasionally mischaracterise cloud compute as "materials consumed", authoritative tax audit rules under Regulation 2900 classify cloud computing, data storage, and software subscription fees as overhead costs rather than physical materials consumed or transformed. Consequently, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method (55% PPA), all overhead of every kind—including cloud computing invoices and SaaS subscriptions—is legally represented inside the 55% notional proxy amount; claiming cloud or subscription invoices separately on top of the 55% PPA constitutes prohibited double-claiming. Cloud computing and software subscription costs are separately claimable only under the Traditional Method. For a team of five engineers with $600,000 of eligible salary base, the Proxy Method yields $330,000 of notional overhead; therefore, if compute-heavy AI training or simulation drives incremental cloud expenditure above 55% of the salary base (exceeding $330,000 in that example), electing the Traditional Method produces a higher tax credit than defaulting to the Proxy Method.

body.text: Subcontractors, Materials Consumed or Transformed, and Restored Capital Property
1. Arm's-Length and Non-Arm's-Length Subcontractors

When a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform eligible SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 80% of the eligible contract payment is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures for the purpose of calculating the section 127 ITC. To substantiate arm's-length contractor claims under CRA audit, claimants must retain statements of work and detailed invoices explicitly identifying the eligible SR&ED activities performed in Canada, and must identify contractor work as such within the Line 244 technical narrative. Where SR&ED work is performed by a non-arm's-length party, the 80% contract inclusion does not apply; instead, qualified expenditures transferred to the claimant from the non-arm's-length performer are reported at Line 508 of Form T661. Conversely, fees paid to accountants, tax advisors, or SR&ED specialists for preparing either the financial or technical portion of the SR&ED claim are prescribed expenditures of a general-administration nature; while deductible as ordinary business expenses, they are strictly ineligible as qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes.
2. Materials Consumed or Transformed

A claimant may include 100% of the cost of materials that are consumed (rendered virtually valueless) or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, such as raw materials destroyed in experimental prototyping runs or chemical reagents consumed in laboratory trials. General office and studio supplies do not qualify as materials consumed or transformed, and claimants must maintain purchase invoices alongside build logs showing which experimental trial consumed each material batch.
3. Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

From January 1, 2014 until December 15, 2024, capital equipment purchases and equipment lease costs were excluded from SR&ED claims under former paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1). Note that while certain outdated secondary commentaries failed to reflect the restoration of lease costs, the official Department of Finance explanatory notes to section 127, enacted Bill C-15, and Version 26 of Form T661 (Lines 350 and 355) confirm that both depreciable capital property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 are fully restored to SR&ED eligibility. Equipment purchased on or before December 15, 2024 remains excluded even if it continues to be used for R&D in 2025 or 2026.

To qualify under the restored rules, depreciable capital property (such as custom test rigs, pilot lines, prototyping cells, tooling, and moulds) must be intended at the time of acquisition to be used all or substantially all—90% or more of its operating time—over its useful life for SR&ED in Canada. Buildings, land, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are statutorily excluded. Furthermore, if capital equipment on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules claw back part or all of the credit.

A critical cash-flow distinction governs the choice between purchasing and leasing R&D equipment after December 15, 2024. When a qualifying CCPC or ECPC purchases R&D equipment within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, it earns the 35% enhanced ITC, but section 127.1 restricts cash refundability on capital expenditures to 40% of the credit (meaning 14.0% of the capital cost is refunded in cash and 21.0% is a non-refundable credit carried back 3 years or forward 20 years). In contrast, when a corporation leases equipment used 90% or more for SR&ED (reported at Line 350 of Form T661), the lease payments are treated as current expenditures, making 100% of the 35% enhanced ITC refundable in cash. Additionally, under the Proxy Method only, if leased equipment (excluding general office equipment or furniture) is used between 50% and under 90% for SR&ED, 50% (half) of the lease cost is eligible on Line 355 of Form T661.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics
The Government Assistance Grind (Subsection 127(11.1))

Under subsection 127(11.1) and the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, any provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (as well as any direct federal or provincial R&D grant, such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program [NRC IRAP] funding) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces ("grinds") the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool before the federal ITC percentage (35% or 15%) is applied. Consequently, while unadjusted summary tables often quote gross additive rates (such as 35% federal + 8% OITC + 3.5% ORDTC = 46.5% gross in Ontario, or 35% federal + 30% Quebec CRIC = 65% gross in Quebec), the actual net combined return is lower because the provincial credit reduces the federal expenditure base: Net Federal ITC = (Qualified SR&ED Expenditures − Provincial Credits and Other Government Assistance) × Federal ITC Rate.

If a provincial credit is non-refundable (such as the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit or the non-refundable tier of the British Columbia SR&ED credit) and a loss-position corporation cannot utilise it immediately, the corporation may formally renounce the non-refundable provincial credit so that it does not grind the 35% refundable federal ITC base.
Provincial Jurisdiction Profiles and Post-Bill C-15 Alignment

Following the federal enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, provincial responses divided between "followers" (such as British Columbia, which expressly aligned with the federal $6,000,000 limit, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration) and "holdouts" or independent reformers (such as Ontario, which automatically restored capital expenditures via federal cross-reference but retained its $3,000,000 OITC cap, and Quebec, which transitioned to the new CRIC regime).
1. Ontario: OITC (Schedule 566) and ORDTC (Schedule 508)

Ontario operates two primary SR&ED tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) that piggyback on federal Form T661. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (and entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5), provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario (attributable to an Ontario permanent establishment) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years based on days in the year over 365). (Historically, the OITC rate was 10% up to $300,000 for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016, and has been 8% up to $240,000 for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016).

Crucially, Ontario did not increase the OITC cap to $6,000,000, and the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is subject to a compounding dual phase-out: the limit is gradually reduced when prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (and is totally eliminated at $800,000) and when prior-year specified taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (and is totally eliminated at $50,000,000). Where a corporation falls inside both phase-out ranges simultaneously, the two surviving fractions multiply rather than taking the lesser of the two separate results: for example, if prior-year taxable income is $700,000 (leaving $1,000,000 of the $3,000,000 limit) and prior-year taxable capital is $30,000,000 (where $25,000,000 minus $5,000,000 leaves 20,000,000/25,000,000 = 80% of the limit), the surviving OITC expenditure limit is $1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000, yielding a maximum OITC of $64,000. Because the OITC definition of qualified expenditure cross-references section 127 of the federal Income Tax Act, Ontario automatically restored 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014 were included at 40%, and those between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 remain excluded). Moreover, while some general summaries assume OITC is restricted to CCPCs, official Ontario Ministry of Finance eligibility rules and comparative provincial analyses confirm that the OITC statute does not require Canadian incorporation or CCPC status, provided the corporation has an Ontario permanent establishment, is not tax-exempt, files Form T661, and its global associated group falls beneath the $800,000 taxable income and $50,000,000 taxable capital ceilings.

The second Ontario credit is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% on June 1, 2016) on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures after deducting the OITC. Unused ORDTC amounts carry back 3 years and forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax. Additionally, Ontario offers the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) for eligible R&D contracts with qualifying research institutes.

In Ontario, the ordering of the calculation is legally prescribed: first, calculate the 8% OITC on the gross Ontario eligible pool; second, subtract the OITC from the Ontario pool to determine the ORDTC base and apply 3.5%; third, subtract both the OITC and the ORDTC (as provincial government assistance) from the federal pool and apply the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate.

body.text: 2. Quebec: Transition from Form RD-1029.7 to the New CRIC Regime

Quebec administers its corporate R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec. For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, corporations claimed the Quebec R&D salary and subcontract credit on Form RD-1029.7 (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages – R&D, with partnership allocations on RL-15 slips and Form RD-1029.7-V, subject to a per-employee exclusion threshold and a $12,500 exclusion threshold for qualified property). However, effective for all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Quebec budget eliminated the fragmented legacy credits—and Revenu Québec rejects Form RD-1029.7 for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—in favour of the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialisation (CRIC). Under the CRIC regime, Revenu Québec provides a 20% to 30% fully refundable tax credit (30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures above the CRIC exclusion threshold, and 20% on excess expenditures, with no upper expenditure cap).
3. British Columbia: Permanent Status and Full Federal Alignment (Bill 2, 2026)

Governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (explained in Bulletin CIT 007), the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit was made permanent under BC Budget 2026, eliminating its former 2027 sunset date. Furthermore, effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, British Columbia expressly aligned its credit with all federal Bill C-15 reforms: first, qualifying corporations that are CCPCs or ECPCs with a BC permanent establishment may claim a 10% fully refundable tax credit (Line 674 of Schedule 5) on the lesser of their BC qualified SR&ED expenditure and their federal expenditure limit, which increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits); second, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor increased to 15,000,000–75,000,000; and third, capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 were restored as BC qualified expenditures. All qualifying corporations (including non-CCPCs/non-ECPCs and CCPCs/ECPCs on spending above the $6,000,000 limit) may claim a 10% non-refundable BC credit (Line 659 of Schedule 5) on BC qualified expenditures less their refundable credit and any amount renounced. The BC credit must be claimed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year. (Separately, BC Budget 2026 introduced a temporary refundable 15% BC Manufacturing and Processing Investment Tax Credit for CCPCs on qualifying buildings, machinery, and equipment acquired between April 1, 2026 and March 31, 2031, up to a maximum credit of $300,000 per corporation).
4. Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29)

Enacted for taxation years beginning on or after January 1, 2021 and filed with the Alberta AT1 corporate tax return on AT1 Schedule 29, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable credit on federal SR&ED-qualifying expenditures (including restored capital expenditures) incurred at a permanent establishment in Alberta up to an annual eligible expenditure cap of $4,000,000 (shared among associated corporations, for a maximum annual credit of $800,000). The IEG is calculated as an 8% base rate on eligible Alberta expenditures up to the corporation's historical base level (the average of the prior two years' eligible Alberta expenditures, rebuilt annually) plus a 12% enhanced rate—producing a 20% combined refundable rate—on incremental Alberta expenditures exceeding that historical base level. The IEG is phased out on a sliding scale for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $50,000,000. To qualify for the IEG, the underlying expenditures must have been validly claimed federally within the 18-month federal SR&ED reporting window.
5. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and the Atlantic Provinces

In Saskatchewan, the R&D Tax Credit provides a 10% refundable credit for CCPCs on the first $2,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures (raised from $1,000,000 for expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024) (and 10% non-refundable for non-CCPCs or spending above the refundable band, up to a $1,000,000 annual credit cap). In Manitoba, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, the provincial R&D tax credit rate is 15%. While Nova Scotia and New Brunswick (as well as Newfoundland and Labrador) provide their 15% credit on a 100% refundable basis to all corporations regardless of size or foreign control (allowing a large corporation in Manitoba or the Maritimes to earn up to 30% gross / 27.75% net combined credits, nearly double the 18.5% gross / 17.975% net return of a large corporation in Ontario), Manitoba's 15% credit is 50% refundable for in-house R&D and 100% refundable for R&D conducted under contract with eligible educational institutions.

body.text: Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Form T661 Mechanics, and Pre-Approval
Administrative Architecture and the New April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process

Unlike dual-agency jurisdictions where an innovation ministry certifies technical eligibility and the revenue authority processes the financial credit, Canada vests both scientific evaluation and financial tax audit authority within a single agency: the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Within the CRA, SR&ED claims are evaluated by scientific/technical specialists (CRA Scientific Advisors / Research and Technology Advisors), who review the technical documentation and conduct site visits to verify whether the claimed work satisfies subsection 248(1), alongside financial reviewers who audit expenditure schedules.

To improve predictability prior to audit, the CRA operates three distinct front-end advisory and pre-approval mechanisms. First, the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) provides a dedicated educational review for first-time SR&ED claimants to establish compliant technical and financial record-keeping systems. Second, the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) service (which replaced the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review [PCPR]) offers free, on-demand consultations to assess potential project eligibility. Third, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process accessible through My Business Account. Through this service, a corporation can request that the CRA formally confirm that its R&D work qualifies for SR&ED before the tax return is filed, with the CRA operating under an eight-week determination standard.
Anatomy of Form T661 (Version 26) and the Technical Narrative Boxes

Accessing federal SR&ED incentives requires filing two prescribed documents together with the income tax return for the year: Form T661, Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim (guided by CRA Publication T4088, Guide to Form T661, with Version 26 of Form T661 updated on May 15, 2026), and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals. Form T661 captures the technical project narratives and calculates deductible and qualified expenditures ending at Line 570, whereas Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) actually claims and computes the dollar Investment Tax Credit.

While Parts 3 through 6 of Form T661 compute the financial claim, Part 2 — Project Information (Section B — Project Descriptions) is the technical heart of the filing where claims are won or lost. A separate Part 2 must be completed for each SR&ED project claimed, and Section B imposes strict word limits across three mandatory technical narrative boxes that should be drafted by or alongside the engineers and scientists who performed the work.

In Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome? — Maximum 350 words), the claimant must articulate the specific scientific or technological uncertainty that existed at the onset of the project, establishing the baseline of publicly available scientific or technological knowledge when work began and explaining why the technical objective could not be resolved by a skilled practitioner applying standard practice or known engineering methods. Claimants must avoid stating commercial business goals, product feature lists, or routine scaling tasks in Line 242. In Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in Line 242? — Maximum 700 words), the claimant must present a chronological, clear, and concise account of the systematic investigation carried out during the taxation year, structured around the formulation of hypotheses designed to reduce the uncertainty, the experiments or analyses conducted to test those hypotheses, the quantitative results obtained, and the conclusions drawn, while explicitly identifying any portion of the experimental work performed by contractors. In Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244? — Maximum 350 words), the claimant must describe the new technical knowledge gained relative to the knowledge base at project onset. Crucially, the CRA's T4088 guide and established jurisprudence confirm that failing to reach a performance or commercial objective does not preclude advancement: proving through systematic testing why a specific technical approach fails under defined constraints constitutes a valid technological advancement. Finally, if a federal agency has designated a project as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant completes Section B of Part 2 on a separate sheet retained in its own records (omitting that sheet from the tax return) and submits an official notification letter with Form T661.

body.text: The 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2) Bar

The most unforgiving procedural rule in Canadian R&D tax law is the 18-month statutory reporting deadline. Under subsection 37(11) (governing the section 37 expenditure pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (governing the section 127 ITC), a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed project and expenditure information within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date. Because a corporation's T2 return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, the statutory SR&ED reporting window closes exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, there is no statutory mechanism to extend this 18-month deadline; missing the 18-month window forfeits both the federal SR&ED claim and all dependent provincial credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC, British Columbia SR&ED credit, and Alberta IEG) in their entirety.

Conversely, filing the SR&ED claim concurrently with the original T2 corporate tax return within 6 months of fiscal year-end cuts CRA processing times by roughly 50% compared to late-window filings, whereas complex or audited claims can take up to 14 months if selected for a detailed technical and financial review. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (such as a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end), if a corporation filed its 2025 claim early under the old $3,000,000 limit or before the CRA updated Form T661 to Version 26 on May 15, 2026 following the March 26, 2026 Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the corporation can file an amended Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 at any time prior to its 18-month deadline (June 30, 2027 for a December 31, 2025 year-end) to capture equipment purchases/leases or spending between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000.

body.text: Judicial Precedents, Case Law, and Audit Defence Standards
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) is framed in broad scientific principles, Canadian courts have established a binding body of jurisprudence to distinguish eligible experimental development from ineligible routine engineering or commercial product development. The foundational judicial authority in Canada is the decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, which established the cumulative five-question legal framework used by the CRA and the courts to evaluate project eligibility under subsection 248(1).

Under the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the first question asks whether there was a scientific or technological uncertainty—meaning an obstacle that could not be resolved on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard engineering practice and experience. In engineering and software development, CRA guidance and practice classify technological uncertainty into four recurring categories: design uncertainty (where it is uncertain whether a specific design can meet required technical specifications), process uncertainty, performance uncertainty, and integration uncertainty (where disparate third-party APIs or system architectures cannot communicate or perform within constraints using established integration methods). The second question asks whether the effort involved formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty. The third question asks whether the overall approach adopted was consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis in chronological iterations rather than unstructured trial-and-error. The fourth question asks whether the overall approach was undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement that increases the stock of technological knowledge, recognizing that experimental failure to achieve a design objective still generates qualifying new knowledge about technological constraints. Finally, the fifth question asks whether contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained were maintained as the work progressed.
Appellate and Tax Court Jurisprudence on Software, Documentation, and Deadlines

Canadian appellate and Tax Court rulings—including the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (alongside foundational Tax Court decisions affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal)—consistently enforce two central audit principles. First, in software and information technology claims (such as Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65), developing novel algorithms, resolving non-linear system limitations, or creating novel architectures qualifies when supported by systematic experimentation, whereas routine coding, standard debugging, and feature development fail the Northwest Hydraulic test. Second, the single largest cause of CRA claim denial is insufficient or inappropriate contemporaneous evidence rather than underlying technical ineligibility. While missing timesheets or summaries can sometimes be reconstructed from contemporaneous engineering artefacts—such as version control commits, project files, timestamped emails, labelled test images, and benchmark logs—maintaining contemporaneous records of hypotheses, test runs, and time allocations as activities occur (and strictly observing the non-extendable 18-month deadline under subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2)) is essential to sustaining an SR&ED claim upon CRA review or Tax Court appeal.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Audit-Ready Compliance Protocols

The legislative overhaul enacted by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, together with the expansion proposed in Federal Budget 2026 on November 5, 2026, has fundamentally transformed the strategic calculus for R&D-intensive enterprises operating in Canada. By doubling the federal enhanced 35% expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit to $2,100,000), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor to 15,000,000–75,000,000, introducing the elective three-year average gross revenue test under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsections 127(10.1) and 127(10.6), and restoring capital equipment and lease eligibility for property acquired after December 15, 2024, Parliament has eliminated the mid-market cliff that previously penalised scaling Canadian innovators.

To capture the full value of these reforms while maintaining audit-ready compliance, corporations and their tax advisors should immediately execute a structured review across six operational dimensions. First, any CCPC or ECPC whose taxation year began after December 15, 2024 (including calendar-year 2025 filers whose 18-month reporting deadline falls on June 30, 2027) that submitted an early 2025 claim under the legacy $3,000,000 limit or omitted R&D capital equipment/leases acquired after December 15, 2024 should file an amended Form T661 (Version 26) and Schedule T2SCH31 prior to its 18-month statutory deadline. Second, asset-heavy CCPCs whose prior-year Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 due to equity or debt financings should model the three-year average gross revenue election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), and ensure that associated CCPC groups (Schedule 49 under subsection 127(10.3)) and consolidated ECPC groups (subsection 127(10.62)) file timely expenditure limit allocation agreements so their limits are not deemed nil.

Third, software, AI, and data-analytics claimants must perform an arithmetic comparison between the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162) every taxation year: because cloud computing and software subscriptions are legally subsumed within the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately under the Proxy Method, compute-intensive teams whose incremental SR&ED cloud infrastructure exceeds 55% of their eligible salary base should elect the Traditional Method. Fourth, for R&D equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 (after applying the ≥ 90% SR&ED use test), financial executives should weigh equipment leasing against outright purchase, recognising that lease payments on Line 350 generate a 100% cash refund of the 35% federal ITC whereas purchased capital property yields a 40% immediate cash refund (14% cash and 21% non-refundable carryforward). Fifth, multi-provincial filers must transition Quebec claims for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 off the rejected Form RD-1029.7 onto the new 20%–30% refundable CRIC regime, leverage British Columbia's permanent 10% refundable credit up to the aligned $6,000,000 cap under Bill 2 (2026), and prepare internal accounting codes for the proposed January 1, 2027 (Budget Day November 5, 2026) expansion of federal SR&ED to regulatory certification studies and IP protection costs alongside the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction. Finally, engineering leads should embed hypothesis-experiment-result tracking into daily development workflows to satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria on Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661, and utilise the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval process through My Business Account (available since April 1, 2026 with an eight-week determination turnaround) whenever embarking on large or unconventional R&D capital deployments.
